# The Wire: Framing, RPC, and Mutual TLS

Everything in Parts II through IV assumed that a client and a server could
exchange bytes. This chapter is about how those bytes are arranged on the
network, how a call is told apart from a reply, how a device proves to a
server which key it holds, and why none of that transport machinery has to be
trusted for the system's security guarantees to hold.

The problem has three layers. At the bottom, a TCP stream is a sequence of
bytes with no message boundaries; something has to say where one message ends
and the next begins. Above that, a remote procedure call (RPC) protocol has to
name the function being called, carry its argument, and match each reply to
the request that produced it. At the top, the two ends have to know who they
are talking to. FOKS inherits the first two layers from the Go implementation
and solves the third with the hostchain from [Chapter 10](10-sigchains.qmd).

## Framing: length-prefixed messages

A *frame* is one message on the wire with an explicit length in front of it.
The receiver reads the length, then reads exactly that many bytes, and knows
it holds one complete message before it tries to interpret any of it. This
is the simplest possible framing and it has a useful side effect: a message
can be validated as a unit, and the receiver can refuse a message before
allocating memory for it.

FOKS frames encode the length as a MessagePack unsigned integer, followed by
the message body, which is a MessagePack array. This is the framing convention
of go-snowpack-rpc, the Go RPC library FOKS uses, whose design descends from
the msgpack-rpc family of protocols (a length-prefixed variant of the original
MessagePack-RPC specification, in which each message is an array whose first
element is a message-type tag). The length marker is held to the same
minimality rule as everything else in FOKS: a length that fits in one byte
must use the one-byte form, and the reader rejects a `uint16` length whose
value would have fit in a `uint8`, and so on. Only the `fixint`, `uint8`,
`uint16`, and `uint32` markers are accepted, and the value is checked against
a ceiling before any buffer is allocated.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Frame length encoding | minimal MessagePack unsigned integer |
| Accepted length markers | `fixint`, `uint8`, `uint16`, `uint32` |
| Default maximum frame | 16 MiB |
| Server memory reserved per frame | 2 × body length, taken from a byte-counted semaphore |

The server-side reader reserves twice the declared length from a process-wide
memory budget before it reads the body ([Chapter 18](18-server-storage.qmd)
describes that budget), so a burst of maximum-size frames from many
connections cannot exhaust memory: the frames simply wait for permits.

## The RPC envelope

Once a frame is in hand, its body is an array. FOKS uses two shapes.

```
CALL_V2   (5 elements)   [ 5, sequence, protocol_id, method_position, payload ]
RESPONSE  (4 elements)   [ 1, sequence, error_or_nil, result ]
```

The first element is a *message type*. The go-snowpack-rpc protocol defines
eight: CALL (0), RESPONSE (1), NOTIFY (2), CANCEL (3), CALL_COMPRESSED (4),
CALL_V2 (5), NOTIFY_V2 (6), and CANCEL_V2 (7). The Rust client emits only
CALL_V2 and the Rust server answers only CALL_V2. NOTIFY and CANCEL messages,
in both versions, are parsed for well-formedness and then discarded, because a
peer never expects a reply to them and closing the connection over a harmless
control message would drop otherwise healthy sessions. CALL_COMPRESSED, on the
other hand, does expect a reply, so receiving one is treated as a fatal
protocol error rather than silently ignored. Nothing in the Rust wire path
compresses.

The second element is the *sequence number*, which pairs a response with its
call. The third and fourth elements of a call identify the function: a 32-bit
*protocol ID* naming a group of related methods (registration, user chains,
Merkle queries, key-value storage, and so on) and a small integer *method
position* within that group. Positions need not be contiguous; the key-value
protocol, for example, uses positions 0 through 18 with 5 and 6 unused. These identifiers
are the dispatch key on the wire, and [Chapter 23](23-compatibility.qmd)
explains how they are extracted mechanically from the Go source rather than
copied by hand.

The Rust server also accepts a six-element call whose trailing element holds
the caller's log tags, because the Go client attaches tags to every call,
including the very first probe of a new host. The extra element is bounded by
the already length-capped frame and is discarded.

### Two codecs, one boundary

[Chapter 9](09-canonical-encoding.qmd) introduced Snowpack, the canonical
MessagePack subset in which every authenticated object has exactly one byte
encoding. The RPC envelope is not Snowpack. It is ordinary MessagePack
produced by Go's `go-codec` library, with named maps, sorted string keys, and
whatever integer widths the encoder chose. A canonical codec would be far too
strict for it, and there is no reason to be strict: nothing in the envelope
is signed or hashed.

The payload slot is different. The argument to a call, and the result in a
response, are canonical Snowpack, and the Rust code keeps the two layers
apart by design:

- The client validates an argument as Snowpack *before* wrapping it in the
  envelope.
- The envelope parser is a separate cursor that knows how to *skip* every
  MessagePack type, including floats, extensions, and maps it never
  interprets, so it can locate the payload slot in a Go-produced frame
  without decoding anything it does not need.
- The response decoder returns the exact bytes of the result slot without
  re-encoding them. Type-specific decoders and verifiers then canonicalize
  every signed or MACed inner object.

The boundary matters because a signature commits to bytes. If the RPC layer
re-serialized a payload, even in a semantically equivalent way, the bytes a
verifier hashed might differ from the bytes the signer hashed. By handing the
payload across untouched, the envelope can be as permissive as Go requires
without endangering the canonical core.

### The DataWrap envelope and the bare-payload protocols

Most FOKS protocols do not put the argument directly in the payload slot.
They wrap it in a two-key map that Go calls `DataWrap`:

```
{ "Data": <canonical Snowpack argument>, "Header": <compatibility header> }
```

The header is a fixed 14-byte string encoding `{V: 1, f1: {Vers: 1}}`, a
versioned union in `go-codec`'s named form. The keys `Data` and `Header` are
written in that order because `go-codec` sorts struct fields, and the Rust
decoder requires exactly that order. When checking a header, the Rust code
accepts any nonzero `Vers`, matching the Go server, which treats only
compatibility generation zero as too old.

Five protocols do not use `DataWrap` at all: the four team protocols
(TeamLoader, TeamAdmin, TeamMember, TeamGuest) and the Kex device-pairing
protocol. Their arguments and results are bare in the payload slot. This is a
quirk of how those particular Go source files were generated, and it was not
documented anywhere. The Rust project discovered it by reading Go's
*generated client code* with an AST parser: each generated method body
declares local variables named `warg` and `tmp`, and whether those variables
are typed as `rpc.DataWrap[...]` reveals whether the method wraps its
argument and result. The finding is rendered into two generated predicates,
keyed by protocol ID, and a Go test using Go's own descriptors confirms the
split. The client selects its response decoder by reading the protocol ID
back out of the request it is about to send.

Even the encoding of "nothing" differs between the two shapes. A wrapped void
result is a `DataWrap` carrying only a header; a bare void result is a
literal nil. A test pins the exact six bytes of a bare void response at
sequence 5: `05 94 01 05 c0 c0`, that is, a one-byte frame length, a
four-element array, RESPONSE, sequence, nil error, nil result.

One more sanctioned deviation: Go encodes an argument struct with zero fields
as an empty array (`0x90`), which canonical Snowpack forbids. The server
accepts exactly that one-byte argument for any method, and the client emits
it where the Go client would.

### Sequence numbers rewritten without re-encoding

Some requests are expensive to build. A chain mutation, for instance, carries
a signed link whose bytes must not change between construction and
transmission. The client therefore prepares every request once with sequence
number zero and *resequences* it just before sending: the framed call is
re-parsed, only the second array element is replaced, and the argument bytes
are copied verbatim into the new frame. The comment in the code states the
purpose plainly: this preserves signed payloads while allowing an
authenticated connection to serve more than one request.

### Exactly-once discipline

An RPC over a pooled connection can fail in three ways: before anything was
written, after the request was written but before a response arrived, or
mid-response. Only the first is safely retryable; in the other two cases the
server may already have acted. The client enforces a small set of rules to
keep every call *exactly-once* from its own point of view.

Each connection carries a `next_sequence` counter. The counter advances only
after a complete response frame with the expected sequence has been read.
An application-level error status counts as a complete frame, because it
arrived with the right sequence and left the stream synchronized. Any other
failure invalidates the connection so that an unread or partial response can
never satisfy a later call.

Idle connections in the pool are probed before reuse. A server closes a
kept-alive session once its own idle timeout elapses; without a probe, the
close would be discovered only when the next request failed mid-flight, and
that request could not be retried safely. So before writing anything, the
client sets the socket non-blocking and calls `peek`. A `WouldBlock` result
means an ordinary idle connection. Zero bytes means the peer closed cleanly.
Any readable byte on an idle connection is a TLS close notification or a
desynchronized stream. In the last two cases the connection is discarded and
a fresh one is opened. The probe is what lets a hardware-backed credential
wait minutes for a person to touch a key and then succeed on its first call
after the pause.

| Pool parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Idle connections per endpoint key | 2 |
| Idle connections total | 16 |
| I/O poll interval for deadline and cancellation checks | 250 ms |

The pool key includes the hostname, port, host ID, a fingerprint of the
client credential, a fingerprint of the trust roots, and which virtual-host
selection protocol was used, so a connection is reused only for the same
peer, the same trust, and the same client key.

## Error encoding

A FOKS status is logically a pair: a numeric code and an optional payload
whose shape depends on the code. On the wire it has two spellings. The Go
server's application layer encodes a status as a positional Snowpack array
`[code, switch]`, where `switch` is a one-arm union keyed by a single
character tag. The Go RPC layer may instead encode a status as a named map
such as `{Sc: 8012, f11: {...}}`. The Rust client's status checker branches
on the first byte: `0xc0` (nil) is success, `0x92` (a two-element array) is
the positional form, and anything else is parsed as a named map.

Four codes receive special handling in the client:

| Code | Name | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| 211 | method not found | protocol ID, method position, and name |
| 1014 | transaction retry | none; a transient conflict the caller may retry (the pairing relay answers each bounded long poll with it, and the client polls again) |
| 1020 | not implemented | none, and any payload is an error |
| 8012 | KV stale cache | a path-version vector telling the client which versions to resync |

The Rust server builds its statuses through the Snowpack encoder, which
reproduces Go's bytes exactly, including `[code, {}]` for a status with no
payload.

## Mutual TLS: identity carried by the certificate

FOKS uses TLS for confidentiality and integrity on the wire, but it does
not use the public certificate-authority system to decide whom to trust.
Instead the hostchain, the signed log of a server's keys described in
[Chapter 10](10-sigchains.qmd), delegates a *TLS certificate authority* key,
and everything else follows from that.

```
           hostchain (signed, Merkle-anchored)
                       |
         delegates     |     delegates
        +--------------+---------------+
        v                              v
  "FOKS delegated TLS CA"      "FOKS client identity CA"
   (Ed25519, self-signed)        (Ed25519, self-signed)
        |                              |
        v                              v
  server leaf certificate       device certificate (7 days)
   for the canonical name        subject key = device Ed25519 key
        |                              |
        v                              v
   client verifies server         server verifies client
   against ONLY this CA           against ONLY this CA
```

### Server identity

First contact with a host goes through the *probe* service over ordinary
WebPKI TLS, that is, TLS verified against the public root certificates a
browser would use. The probe response contains the signed hostchain, the
signed public zone (the list of service endpoints), and the signed Merkle
root, each of which the client verifies independently as
[Chapter 13](13-client-verification.qmd) describes. The probe call is not
pooled and is suitable only for discovery data that will be authenticated by
other means.

Once the hostchain is verified, the client builds a trust store containing
*only* the host's own delegated CA certificates and uses that store for every
other service: registration, user chains, Merkle queries, key-value storage,
and realtime chat. The public CA system is out of the loop. On the server,
the delegated CA is a self-signed Ed25519 certificate derived from a host
purpose key, and the same DER bytes are what the hostchain commits to. A
server that presents a certificate not chained to the CA in its own host
chain is rejected, no matter which public authority vouches for it.

### Client identity

Authenticated services require a *client certificate*, which is TLS's
mechanism for the client to prove possession of a key during the handshake.
FOKS does not invent a separate login protocol for ordinary RPC. A device's
Ed25519 key is already enrolled in the user's signature chain; the
certificate is a thin X.509 wrapper around that key.

1. The device calls the public, unauthenticated
   `getClientCertChain(uid, device_id)` method.
2. The server checks that the device is an active credential owner (and that
   any single-sign-on policy still permits access, see
   [Chapter 22](22-sso.qmd)), then issues a certificate whose subject public
   key *is* the device's Ed25519 key, signed by the host's client identity
   CA. If a certificate with more than a day of validity remaining already
   exists, it is returned instead of issuing a new one.
3. The client wraps its device seed as a PKCS#8 Ed25519 private key,
   confirms the key matches the certificate, and presents the chain in the
   TLS handshake.
4. The server's authenticated listener verifies the chain against the client
   CA. After the handshake, it parses the peer certificate, requires an
   Ed25519 subject key (OID 1.3.101.112), looks the certificate up in the
   database to find the credential it was issued to, and **re-checks that
   the public key in the certificate equals the key inside the credential's
   entity ID**. The kind of credential (software device, delegated subkey,
   backup key, bot token) then gates which routes the connection may call.

| Certificate parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Validity | 7 days |
| Reused if remaining validity exceeds | 1 day |
| `not_before` backdated for clock skew | 5 minutes |
| Serial number | 20 random bytes, top bit cleared, never all zero |

The re-check in step 4 is a small thing with a large consequence. The TLS
library has already verified the chain; the database lookup has already
found a binding. Comparing the certificate's key to the entity ID closes the
gap in which a database row could be associated with the wrong certificate,
and it means the server's notion of "who is calling" is the same public key
that appears in the user's chain, not merely a certificate the server once
signed.

### Why "untrusted transport" still holds

The threat model in [Chapter 1](01-problem.qmd) says the server is not
trusted, and the reader may wonder how that squares with a TLS design in
which the server issues the client's certificate. The answer is that TLS
here is a *convenience and a first line of defense*, not the basis of any
security claim. Every object that matters, a chain link, a Merkle root, a
key box, an encrypted directory entry, carries its own signature or
authentication tag, made with keys that the server never sees. A server that
forged a client certificate could open a connection, but it could not sign a
chain link as that device, because the signing key is not in the
certificate. A server that lied about its own TLS CA would be caught by the
hostchain, which is signed by keys the client pinned at first contact and
which the Merkle tree makes impossible to rewrite silently. TLS keeps
passive observers out and gives the server a cheap way to reject
unauthorized callers early. The inner signatures are what the system
actually depends on.

## The local IPC protocol, briefly

The agent described in [Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd) talks to its front ends (the
command-line tool, the desktop, and the MCP server) over a Unix domain
socket, and that protocol is deliberately different from the FOKS wire
protocol. It is local, never crosses a network, and carries nothing that is
signed, so it optimizes for simplicity and bounded resource use rather than
canonicality.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Framing | 4-byte big-endian length, then JSON |
| Maximum message | 1 MiB |
| Envelope reserve | 32 KiB |
| Maximum KV payload per frame | 700 KiB |
| Protocol version | 30 |

Byte payloads are carried as base64 strings rather than JSON integer arrays.
The module documentation works out why: a uniformly random byte costs about
3.57 characters as an integer-array element (digits plus a separator,
averaged over the byte distribution) but a fixed 1.33 as base64. From the
1 MiB frame cap, the 32 KiB reserved for everything that travels beside the
payload (version, correlation ID, store reference, path, timing), and the
base64 ratio, the maximum payload per frame is derived as 700 KiB, and a
test confirms the worst-case envelope still fits. A request that asks for
more is refused as invalid; nothing is ever truncated. Every message carries
a version and a correlation ID, and a response binds to its request's ID.
Frames are held in zeroizing buffers. Chapter 19 covers the security checks
on the socket itself: ownership, permissions, and peer credentials.

## Where to look

- `foks-rpc`: `lib.rs` (framing, call and response encoders, `resequence_call`,
  the compatibility header, the skipping cursor), `server.rs` (inbound
  message classification, the six-element call, the empty-array argument),
  `response.rs` and `status.rs` (status encoding and decoding),
  `generated/protocol_ids.rs` and `generated/status_codes.rs`.
- `foks-client`: `transport.rs` (connection pool, `is_reusable`,
  `call_current`, TLS client configuration), `host.rs`
  (`authenticated_tls_roots`).
- `foks-server`: `pki/host_tls.rs` (the two CAs and listener configurations),
  `auth/principal.rs` (certificate-to-credential binding), `net/session.rs`
  (certificate issuance, asynchronous frame reading, memory permits).
- `foks-agent-proto`: `frame.rs`, `base64_bytes.rs`, `message.rs`.
- `tools/foks-protocol-sync`: `internal/extract/extract.go`
  (`bindingUsesDataWrap`).
